ledger.sentence: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation, and it is also used in hepatic encephalopathy, a liver condition that causes confusion.
The NHS says it draws water into the bowel to make poo softer, and that it takes at least 2 days to work.
Treating constipation.
Treating hepatic encephalopathy, a liver disease that causes confusion, tremor and a decreased level of consciousness.
The NHS says lactulose relieves constipation by drawing water into the bowel, which makes poo softer.
Osmotic laxatives such as lactulose retain water in the bowel, which increases the volume of the stools and makes them softer and easier to pass, according to local NHS laxative guidance.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says lactulose takes at least 2 days to work, and that anyone whose constipation has not improved after 4 or 5 days should talk to a doctor.
The NHS says diarrhoea, particularly with high amounts, is a very common side effect.
Bloating and wind are also common, and these effects are usually mild and do not last long.
The NHS says serious side effects are rare, and that anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, is possible in rare cases.
Long-term use can lead to prolonged diarrhoea and an imbalance of body salts (electrolytes).
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.
The NHS says most people aged 14 and over can use lactulose, and that children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it.
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose or a similar medicine, galactosaemia, lactose intolerance and galactose or fructose allergies as reasons to avoid it.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage that is not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says lactulose increases gas and bloating, which can make IBS worse.
For people with diabetes, the NHS says usual constipation amounts should have little or no effect on blood sugar, but high amounts taken for many months might.
The NHS says lactulose can be taken during pregnancy and is not harmful to the baby, and that breastfeeding is fine if a doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy.
The NHS says contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy if lactulose makes someone vomit or causes severe diarrhoea.
A doctor reviews constipation that has not improved after 4 or 5 days of lactulose, according to the NHS.
For hepatic encephalopathy, treatment is directed by a clinician and diarrhoea-related dehydration is a concern.
